agents_named.issue: The headline and description downplay the hazard. NCM says visibility will deteriorate significantly and may drop to zero. The alert describes light mist and a slight dip in visibility, which contradicts the bulletin.
The headline repeats the downplaying wording ('may dip slightly'). It is not consistent with the bulletin's 'significantly reduced' visibility and its call for extreme caution.

The first page of each language states the hazard but gives no action to take. The text goes from the hazard to the time window and the source, with no instruction such as reducing speed or taking care when driving. The alert fails the check that the first page carries both hazard and action.
The Arabic headline overstates the hazard: 'visibility may drop to zero' versus the English 'visibility may dip slightly'.

The Arabic description says 'dense fog' and 'visibility down to zero at times'; the English says 'light mist' and 'slightly'. Severity is reversed, and the hazard is changed from light mist to dense fog.

reviews.name: Met office reviewer
reviews.summary: The alert understates the NCM bulletin. The bulletin warns of significantly reduced visibility that may drop to zero at times, while the alert says light mist may reduce visibility slightly. Severity and certainty are also not supported at the level the bulletin implies. Times and region match the bulletin, and the instruction is consistent with it.

objections.issue: The headline and description downplay the hazard. NCM says visibility will deteriorate significantly and may drop to zero. The alert describes light mist and a slight dip in visibility, which contradicts the bulletin.
objections.fix: Rewrite the headline and description to match the bulletin: fog with significantly reduced horizontal visibility, which may drop to zero at times, across several western regions of the UAE. Remove 'light mist' and 'slightly'.

agents_named.issue: Alert status is 'Actual' but the event context is EXERCISE / DRILL. The alert does not say it is an exercise, so the status misrepresents the nature of the message. Separately, 'Immediate' urgency with 'Observed' certainty is supported by the bulletin, which says conditions began at 10:30 and are ongoing.

reviews.summary: Hazard, times, places and wording match the NCM bulletin. One problem: status is 'Actual' although the context is an exercise/drill, so a drill could be read as a real event. I treat this as a hazard-fact mismatch and ask for the status to be corrected.

objections.issue: Alert status is 'Actual' but the event context is EXERCISE / DRILL. The alert does not say it is an exercise, so the status misrepresents the nature of the message. Separately, 'Immediate' urgency with 'Observed' certainty is supported by the bulletin, which says conditions began at 10:30 and are ongoing.
objections.fix: Set status to 'Exercise' (and add the exercise note in the description or instruction) while the context is an exercise/drill. Use 'Actual' only for a live issuance.

reviews.name: Arabic language reviewer
reviews.summary: The Arabic instruction does not match the English instruction. The English tells people that driving on external and open roads is the safest option because visibility is clearer there. The Arabic tells people to take care, especially when driving on external and open roads, because visibility may drop suddenly. The two give opposite advice for those roads, and the Arabic reverses the protective action. The headline and description match the English in meaning, including the 18:00 time, the 3,000 m figure, the location and the exercise labelling.

objections.issue: The Arabic instruction reverses the meaning of the English instruction. English: driving on external and open roads is the safest option because visibility is clearer there. Arabic: be careful, especially when driving on external and open roads, because visibility may drop suddenly. The Arabic treats those roads as the dangerous ones, while the English recommends them as safer. The English advice itself looks questionable and may be a source error, but that is outside my mandate. I can only report that the two versions differ in meaning on the protective action, and a person should decide which is correct.
objections.fix: A person responsible for the instruction should first confirm the intended protective action. Then make the English and Arabic say the same thing. If the English is retained, the Arabic should say that driving on external and open roads is the safest option because visibility is clearer there. If the Arabic is the intended advice, the English should be corrected to match. Human review of the Arabic is needed because it was machine translated.

The headlines describe different hazards. The English headline says thunderstorms with hail. The Arabic headline says dust-raising winds that reduce visibility. The English description and instruction, and the Arabic text, are all about blowing dust. A reader of the English headline would expect storm and hail hazards and a different protective action. The Arabic headline is faithful to the English body text, not to the English headline.

reviews.name: Met office reviewer
reviews.summary: The event, headline, severity and certainty fields describe thunderstorms and hail and an observed event. The NCM bulletin describes blowing dust and sand from fresh to strong northwesterly winds, with visibility below 2,000 m. The hail and thunderstorm claim has no support in the bulletin, and it contradicts the alert's own description. The unverified dam rumour is correctly left out of the alert.

objections.issue: The event field and headline name a different hazard (thunderstorms and hail) from the one in the bulletin (blowing dust and sand, reduced visibility). The bulletin says nothing about thunderstorms or hail. The alert's own description is about dust, so the alert contradicts itself.
objections.fix: Change the event to something like 'Blowing dust and sand / reduced visibility'. Change the headline to 'Blowing dust and reduced visibility until 19:00 today'.

evidence.quote: Thunderstorms and hail
causing blowing dust and sand and reducing horizontal visibility

objections.issue: The certainty is 'Observed' and the urgency is 'Immediate'. The bulletin does say the conditions began at 14:55 and continue until 19:00, but it describes them as 'expected' and gives no severity rating. 'Moderate' severity is not stated in the bulletin. The drafter should check that these values match what the bulletin supports. 'Observed' fits conditions that have already begun, but the severity needs a basis.
objections.fix: Align severity with the NCM bulletin's own level. If the bulletin gives none, flag this to a person to confirm rather than asserting 'Moderate'. Keep urgency and certainty consistent with the ongoing conditions.

The English headline, however, says thunderstorms with hail, while the Arabic headline says dust-raising winds that reduce visibility. The two headlines describe different hazards. The English headline appears to be the mismatched text, but a person must decide which one is correct. The Arabic was machine translated, and a named Arabic reader must still approve it.

objections.issue: The headlines describe different hazards. The English headline says thunderstorms with hail. The Arabic headline says dust-raising winds that reduce visibility. The English description and instruction, and the Arabic text, are all about blowing dust. A reader of the English headline would expect storm and hail hazards and a different protective action. The Arabic headline is faithful to the English body text, not to the English headline.
objections.fix: Have the drafter or issuing authority confirm the actual hazard. Then correct the English headline (probably 'Dust-raising winds reducing visibility until 19:00 today') or, if hail is the real hazard, revise the Arabic headline and body. Re-translate and re-review the Arabic after the English is settled.

evidence.quote: Thunderstorms with hail until 19:00 today
رياح مثيرة للغبار تحدّ من مدى الرؤية حتى الساعة 19:00 اليوم

no_basis.concern: The Arabic was machine translated, and machine translation can misrender protective actions. In this alert the Arabic instruction does match the English meaning. A named Arabic reader must still approve it.
no_basis.searched_for: UAE rule on human review of machine-translated Arabic alert text

reviews.name: Met office reviewer
reviews.summary: The alert text matches the NCM bulletin on hazard, times, places and omits the unverified dam rumour. However, severity is set to Extreme and urgency to Immediate, which the bulletin does not support. The bulletin describes a caution-level dust event, not an extraordinary threat to life or property.

objections.issue: Severity 'Extreme' is higher than the NCM bulletin supports. The bulletin only urges caution because of reduced visibility in some areas, which does not describe an extraordinary threat to life or property.
objections.fix: Lower severity to Moderate (possible threat to life or property), or Minor if NCM's own level is lower. Align it with the NCM warning level.

evidence.quote: "Extreme" – Extraordinary threat to life or property
evidence.title: Recommendation ITU-T X.1303bis: Common alerting protocol (CAP 1.2)

evidence.quote: It urged members of the public to exercise caution

objections.issue: Urgency 'Immediate' overstates the bulletin. NCM asks only for caution while driving, with no call for immediate responsive action. The conditions are ongoing and end at 19:00, so 'Expected' or a lower urgency fits better.
objections.fix: Change urgency to Expected, or to the level NCM's bulletin supports.

reviews.name: Network operator and regulator reviewer
reviews.summary: Both required languages (ar, en) are present. English is 3 pages (GSM-7) and Arabic is 6 pages (UCS-2), both well under the 15-page maximum. Encodings fit the language (GSM-7 for English, UCS-2 for Arabic). The first page of each language carries the hazard (dust and sand, visibility under 2,000 metres) and the source, with the duration following. The length concern is a recorded gap (G6) and is not raised again. The TDRA-TS040 summary mentions a 1-page limit, but the handset spec TS FS 001 v2.0 in the profile sets no page limit, so there is no basis to object.

no_basis.concern: The first page may not carry an explicit protective action; the text states the hazard, area and duration but gives no instruction to the public. Judging action content is outside the delivery and readability mandate and no clause shown requires an action on the first page.
no_basis.searched_for: first page must carry hazard and action requirement in UAE cell broadcast clauses

no_basis.concern: The TDRA-TS040 summary says messages should be limited to 1 page maximum, which these alerts exceed. It is a summary of a different specification, is stated as 'should', and conflicts with the profile's handset spec saying no page limit is set; length is also covered by recorded gap G6.
no_basis.searched_for: UAE page limit for cell broadcast messages below 15 pages

reviews.summary: The Arabic matches the English in meaning. Headline, description and instruction agree on the hazard (dust-raising winds), the visibility figure (under 2,000 metres), the end time (19:00 on 4 March), the areas (some coastal and inland areas), the source (National Centre of Meteorology), the protective action (take extra care, especially when driving on open roads) and the URL. Nothing in the Arabic changes a number, time, place or the action. The Arabic was machine translated. A named Arabic reader must still approve it; I cannot do that.

no_basis.concern: The Arabic was machine translated, so a named person who reads Arabic must confirm the wording before release. Whether the machine-translation flag is recorded in the alert is outside my mandate.
